study.title: Different Degree Centrality Changes in the Brain after Acupuncture on Contralateral or Ipsilateral Acupoint in Patients with Chronic Shoulder Pain: A Resting-State fMRI Study
study.study_design: Randomized, controlled trial using fMRI scan to evaluate the effectiveness and mechanism of a single acupuncture session contralateral or ipsilateral to the CSP
study.randomization: The randomization list was generated by use of the SPSS19.0 software and patients were randomly assigned to treatment groups in a 1:1 ratio
study.blinding: The patients, outcome assessors, and statisticians were blinded to treatment allocation
study.population: Patients with chronic shoulder pain recruited in outpatient clinics from the department of acupuncture at Beijing Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine Affiliated to Capital Medical University
study.inclusion_criteria: (i) left-sided shoulder pain for at least 6 weeks and no more than 1 year, (ii) age between 45 and 65 years, (iii) an average pain score of 50 mm or more on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS) in the past week, (iv) the ability to communicate in Chinese, and (v) no history of shoulder surgery
study.exclusion_criteria: (i) neurological disorders causing shoulder pain, (ii) referred pain from the cervical spine, (iii) osteoarthritis of the gleno-humeral joint or systemic bone and joint disorder (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis), (iv) receiving acupuncture or other current therapy involving analgesics in the preceding month, (v) overt psychiatric illness, (vi) drug or alcohol abuse, and (vii) structural MRI abnormalities in the brain and any contraindications for magnetic resonance imaging scans

arms.dropouts: Four patients in the ipsilateral group were excluded due to excessive head motion or not receiving the second fMRI scan

conditions.scan_context: Resting-state fMRI; patients lay supine, instructed to close their eyes, keep awake, and move as little as possible

extraction_notes.note: Exact baseline VAS and CMS values for each group are not reported in this paper; the paper states 'Baseline and clinical outcome characteristics had previously been described in detail [19]' (Zhang et al. 2018, Journal of Pain Research). Only change scores and between-group comparisons are reported here.
No quantitative deqi/sensory response scores are reported. Deqi was intended and described qualitatively but no instrument (e.g., MASS, MGQ) was used or reported.
No expectancy, credibility, or treatment blinding success measures were reported beyond the statement that patients were told they would receive an effective intervention.
No adverse events section is present in the paper. It is unclear whether no adverse events occurred or whether they were not assessed/reported.
Trial registration number is not reported in the paper.

The paper states 24 patients were enrolled and randomized (12 per group), but 4 in the ipsi-group were excluded. Additionally, 3 patients (group not specified) were excluded for head motion exceeding 3 mm or 3 degrees. Final analyzed N is stated as 20 for neuroimaging. It is unclear whether the 3 motion exclusions are among the 4 ipsi-group exclusions or additional. The clinical n analyzed may differ from neuroimaging n analyzed; the paper references clinical outcomes from the prior study [19].

Supplementary Table 1 ('significant differences in degree centrality between two groups') is referenced in the paper but not provided in the extracted PDF. Full between-group results including medial frontal gyrus data may be in the supplement.
Supplementary Figure 1 (weighted version of DC results) is referenced but not provided in the extracted PDF. The paper states these results are 'nearly identical' to binary version results.

Figures 2, 3, 4, and 5 contain neuroimaging visualizations. Figure 2 shows multiple threshold binary DC results. Specific coordinate values for thresholds other than r0=0.25 are not tabulated in the text; only the primary threshold (r0=0.25) results appear in Table 1.

The paper states flip angle = 90 degrees and 33 slices for the fMRI acquisition, but does not report the total scan duration in explicit minutes/volumes. The first 10 images were removed during preprocessing.

The paper reports a grey matter mask with 'grey matter probabilities larger than 20%' using the SPM8 tissue prior template, though the preprocessing used SPM12. This potential inconsistency is noted but not resolved in the paper.

Correlation threshold r0=0.10 is listed in the methods as one of six thresholds used, but Figure 2 shows only r0=0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, and 0.35. It is unclear whether r0=0.10 results are included in Figure 2 or the supplement.

The paper states all 24 patients 'underwent fMRI in baseline.' The final neuroimaging sample of 20 (12 contra + 8 ipsi) reflects post-exclusion numbers. The contra-group n=12 for neuroimaging is inferred from 'twelve patients assigned minus zero excluded'; the paper does not explicitly state this number for the contra-group's final neuroimaging sample.
No needle size (gauge/length) is reported beyond 'Huatuo, Suzhou Medical Co. Ltd., Jiangsu, China' for the needles used.
Practitioner qualifications, training, or years of experience are not described.
